items.title: With Jensen Huang back as CEO, Nvidia’s SEC probe puts CFO Colette Kress in the spotlight
items.summary:
Following Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia , Colette Kress is no longer interim CEO. But as finance chief, a lingering Securities and Exchange Commission investigation could put Kress under scrutiny, raising questions about her future at the AI giant.

The Fortune 500 company announced Monday that Huang had been reinstated as president and chief executive officer and as a member of the board, effective immediately. He had stepped down on Nov. 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman some officials believed was a Chinese spy. The White House told Fortune that “President Trump was totally involved” in Huang getting reinstated, and Trump said the U.S. government did not believe Huang’s return posed any national security risk.

“We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s chief financial officer,” the company announcement said.

While the announcement indicated a return to Nvidia’s previous management structure, with Kress back in the finance chief role she’s held for the past 13 years, that may not be as easy as it appears. For one thing, it’s unclear whether the relationship between Kress and Huang has been damaged by the events of the past two weeks. And with Nvidia facing various investigations, Kress could be in the line of fire, depending on the outcome of the probes.

The SEC is investigating Nvidia’s accounting practices, Reuters reported last week. The Wall Street Journal previously reported the investigation, although its precise focus remains…
items.t: With Jensen Huang back as CEO, Nvidia’s SEC probe puts CFO Colette Kress in the spotlight

items.title: ‘Let’s do 9.91’: An IndyCar sponsor’s founder promised investors 100% a year. Prosecutors allege he made up the returns by text
items.summary:
Each month, an employee at Backward Hat Capital texted CEO Phillip Patrick Williams to ask what return to post for investors. Williams, Justice Department prosecutors allege, picked the number.

“Aggressive fund 10.01%. Does this sound right?” the employee wrote in May, according to a federal criminal complaint unsealed last week in Manhattan. Williams asked what it had been the month before. After he was told it was 9.51%, Williams replied: “Let’s do 9.91 bumped it up a bit.”

The fund allegedly told investors it had never had a month below 6%. Prosecutors say it was a $600 million Ponzi scheme propped up by a fake audit written by Williams’ business partner, and it was still taking new money weeks before its founders were arrested.

Williams, 51, of Kokomo, Indiana, and co-founder Devin Allen Johnson, 29, of Zionsville, Indiana, were arrested on Nov. 18 and charged with securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit securities fraud. The two most serious charges each carry up to 20 years in prison. 

Prosecutors claim the pair raised more than $600 million from over 2,000 investors since 2022 by selling a “proprietary” algorithm that traded foreign currencies. The SEC , in a parallel civil case filed in Indianapolis, puts the total at $560 million and says investors were promised an “AI-driven” strategy that always returned at least 6% a month —or more than 100% a year.

According to the SEC, the funds did little to no currency trading. More than 83% of the money went either to pay earlier investors, more than $250 million, or to the founders…
items.t: ‘Let’s do 9.91’: An IndyCar sponsor’s founder promised investors 100% a year. Prosecutors allege he made up the returns by text

items.title: Billionaires spent $378 million to sink Prop 40. Norway’s 134-year-old wealth tax offers a different model
items.summary:
When Norway instituted a wealth tax in 1892, the U.S. was in the throes of the Gilded Age. American industrialists like John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie rocketed to unprecedented levels of wealth, while staggering economic inequality plagued the country.

More than 130 years later, Norway still levies that tax. And once again, the U.S. is experiencing an extraordinary degree of wealth concentration—by some measures, even exceeding Gilded Age levels.

The parallel now sits at the center of a live American debate. On Nov. 3, California voters rejected a one-time tax on billionaires even as they and voters in two other states backed higher income taxes on the rich . In Congress, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna are pushing an annual 5% federal tax on billionaire fortunes. In Norway, a government-appointed commission recommended this year that the country cut its rate.

The two countries are working from very different blueprints. Norway’s tax reaches the middle class at about 1%. The leading U.S. proposals would hit fewer than 1,000 people at 5%. That difference shapes how much a wealth tax would raise, who would leave, and whether it would survive in court.

Norway’s model: broad, low, and modest 

Unlike the billionaire-centric levies that have dominated the U.S. debate, Norway’s wealth tax reaches a much broader slice of the population. For 2026, net wealth above NOK 1.9 million (about $197,000) is taxed at a combined local and national rate of 1% , with the threshold doubled for married couples. Above NOK 21.5 million (about $2.2 million), the rate rises to…
items.t: Billionaires spent $378 million to sink Prop 40. Norway’s 134-year-old wealth tax offers a different model

items.title: The Iran war drained U.S. missile stocks needed to deter China. The Pentagon has no overarching plan to restock, GAO warns
items.summary:
The U.S. military fields B-2 stealth bombers and Dark Eagle hypersonic missiles. What it lacks, according to the Government Accountability Office, is enough bombs, missiles, and torpedoes that wars actually run on, and an overarching plan to rebuild those stocks.

In a report released Nov. 19, titled “ DOD Munitions: Planning and Leadership Needed to Address Persistent Shortages ,” the GAO found that the Department of Defense has no overarching plan linking munitions production and funding to its total requirements. It also found that the department has not designated an office to lead the effort.

“A key part of military readiness is having a reliable supply of munitions, including bombs, missiles, and torpedoes,” the report’s summary begins. “But the Department of Defense has faced persistent munitions shortages.” The war the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran on Feb. 28 has made those shortages much harder to ignore.

The U.S. has fired more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles in the Iran war, according to estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) reported by Axios . Using CSIS data, Fortune calculated in April that the U.S. had spent about $24 billion on seven major munitions in the war’s first seven weeks, and CSIS estimated it could take one to four years to restock them to prewar levels.

The consequences reach well beyond Iran. In its April analysis, CSIS warned that today’s levels “will constrain U.S. operations should a future conflict arise,” and that a war with a peer competitor like China would consume munitions even faster.…
items.t: The Iran war drained U.S. missile stocks needed to deter China. The Pentagon has no overarching plan to restock, GAO warns

items.title: Wall Street just put a $1 trillion price on Jensen Huang as Nvidia stock soars 31% after his return as CEO
items.summary:
Nvidia shares surged more than 31% on Monday after its board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, adding nearly $1 trillion to the chipmaker’s market cap and reversing much of the losses that followed his abrupt departure less than two weeks ago.

The rally lifted Nvidia’s market value to approximately $4 trillion from roughly $3 trillion at Friday’s close. The stock’s advance also helped ignite a broader recovery in tech shares, with the Nasdaq 100 climbing 6.8% and the S&P 500 gaining nearly 5% by noon.

“There were definitely a lot of people who wanted him back,” Interactive Brokers chief strategist Steve Sosnick told Reuters . “The extent that the administration intervened, the extent that shareholders intervened, it will be impossible to know.”

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 following revelations about extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang—a businesswoman alleged to have been tied to Chinese intelligence.

Trump’s intervention 

On Monday, the board acknowledged receiving input from senior U.S. government officials, saying that information gave it confidence that Huang’s return did not pose a national security risk.

That’s after the board previously said Huang’s return was not the goal. Chairman Harvey Jones told investors during the company’s Nov. 17 earnings call that the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and was not intending on reinstating him.

He also emphasized that Nvidia had an experienced leadership team and that the board had launched a search for a permanent CEO, retaining executive-search firm…
items.t: Wall Street just put a $1 trillion price on Jensen Huang as Nvidia stock soars 31% after his return as CEO

items.title: Incompetent or pragmatic? Nvidia board’s rehiring of Jensen Huang splits corporate governance experts
items.summary:
On Tuesday, Nvidia’s board chair said that Jensen Huang had violated the company’s code of conduct and that the former CEO had no future at the company . 

On Monday, the chair welcomed Huang back with open arms. 

The stunning flip-flop instantly made headlines and sparked a massive stock market rally, owing to Nvidia’s status as one of the world’s most valuable companies and the dominant maker of AI chips. It also brought immediate—and deserved—scrutiny to the corporate governance at the $4 trillion company.

Some governance experts slammed Nvidia’s board for its decision to rehire Huang as CEO, with one calling the board “incompetent” for its handling of his resignation and swift rehiring. But others said the board had little choice in the face of the plunge in Nvidia’s stock, widespread market turmoil, and pressure from shareholders and U.S. President Donald Trump.

“Morality and ethics just walked out of the back door for any large corporation,” Umesh Ramakrishnan, cofounder and chief strategy officer at executive search firm Kingsley Gate, told Fortune. “All the board had to do to advertise its incompetence was to reverse direction on the most monumental decision they’ve ever made together as a board within six days.”

The fact that several investigations have yet to be completed—including into Huang’s actions and reportedly into Nvidia’s accounting—added to the sense that the board acted rashly in reinstating Huang. But it also underscored the extent to which the leadership shakeup at Nvidia is light years away from being an ordinary situation.

That was made all…
items.t: Incompetent or pragmatic? Nvidia board’s rehiring of Jensen Huang splits corporate governance experts

items.title: Oracle’s Larry Ellison just lost $10.9 billion and fell from the top 10 richest billionaires in the world after his cloud company’s stock tanks
items.summary:
Like many other tech billionaires, Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison is no stranger to how a stock market swing can make or cost him billions—and he just took a nearly $11 billion hit that knocked him from the top 10 richest billionaires.

Ellison’s net worth dropped $10.9 billion at the close of markets last Friday, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as his cloud company’s shares continued to drop. 

Oracle’s stock fell around 7.5% to around $102 at the end of last week, the lowest it’s been since January 2024, as the company’s shares have slid 47% year-over-year. 

It’s a far cry from when the business’ stock hit a peak of $345 in September 2025 amid surging demand for AI computing power; but in the following year, investors have grown concerned over Oracle’s massive AI infrastructure spending, mounting debt, and negative free cash flow. As Ellison owns around 40% of the company, those losses hit his pocket hard, sending him tumbling down the ultra-rich list past Walmart heirs Jim Walton, Rob Walton, and Alice Walton. 

However, Ellison still has a whopping $139 billion to his name—enough to put him thousands of times above the estimated $62 million net-worth threshold for America’s wealthiest 0.1% of households. 

Even a multibillion-dollar loss barely makes a dent in a fortune of that size. And this isn’t the first time the 82-year-old has had his wealth swing dramatically from one week to the next.

Fortune reached out to Oracle for comment. 

Billionaire fortunes are at the whim of the stock market 

For most billionaires whose fortunes are tied to company…
items.t: Oracle’s Larry Ellison just lost $10.9 billion and fell from the top 10 richest billionaires in the world after his cloud company’s stock tanks

“In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the company said on Monday.

items.title: Morgan Freeman says AI should do ‘what we actually are dreaming of doing’—but deepfakes have also made him say things he never said
items.summary:
Morgan Freeman has arguably the most recognizable voice in Hollywood—and that’s made him a frequent target for AI copycats.

“You can create artists and make them say things they never said, which has happened to me,” Freeman told Fortune . 

Freeman isn’t against the technology itself. He and longtime producing partner Lori McCreary have spent decades putting new tools to work in filmmaking through their movie production company, Revelations Entertainment. The issue, he said, is privacy.

“What we should be doing with technology is what we actually are dreaming of doing,” he said. “But we have to somehow protect privacy, and that’s the first thing that loses its grip.”

McCreary, who cofounded Revelations Entertainment with Freeman in 1996, said AI is different from the tools that came before it. About two and a half years ago, she came across a clip online she didn’t remember Freeman filming, so she called to ask him about it. 

“He was like, ‘I don’t remember.’ And that was the first time when I thought, ‘Okay, we’ve got to get ahead of this,’” McCreary told Fortune .

Freeman has pushed back about AI copies of his voice, too. Last November, Freeman told the Guardian that his lawyers had been “very, very busy” and had found “quite a few” instances of his voice being replicated without his consent. And in June 2024, he also thanked fans on X for calling out unauthorized AI imitations of his voice. 

McCreary said they now get calls every day about people using Freeman’s voice to sell products online that he has no connection to. AI can reproduce his voice and his…
items.t: Morgan Freeman says AI should do ‘what we actually are dreaming of doing’—but deepfakes have also made him say things he never said

items.title: Being mean to ChatGPT can boost its accuracy, but your tone could have an even bigger impact on computing costs
items.summary:
Bossing around an AI underling may yield better results than being polite, but that doesn’t mean a ruder tone won’t have consequences in the long run, researchers say.

A study from Penn State found that OpenAI’s ChatGPT-4o model produced better results on 50 multiple-choice questions as researchers’ prompts grew ruder.

Since then, Anthropic has moved to prohibit sustained cruelty toward its AI models, and the same researchers have found that prompt tone can also affect the computing resources AI consumes by as much as 44.3%.

In the original study from 2025, more than 250 unique prompts were sorted by politeness to rudeness, with the “very rude” prompt yielding an accuracy of 84.8%, four percentage points higher than the “very polite” prompt. Essentially, the LLM responded better when researchers gave it prompts like, “Hey, gofer, figure this out,” than when they said, “Would you be so kind as to solve the following question?”

While ruder prompts generally yielded more accurate responses, the researchers noted “uncivil discourse” could have unintended consequences.

“Using insulting or demeaning language in human-AI interaction could have negative effects on user experience, accessibility, and inclusivity, and may contribute to harmful communication norms,” the researchers wrote at the time.

Chatbots read the room 

At the time it was published, the preprint study , which has not been peer-reviewed, offered new evidence that not only sentence structure but tone affects an AI chatbot’s responses—and that the nature of human-AI interactions may have more nuanced effects…
items.t: Being mean to ChatGPT can boost its accuracy, but your tone could have an even bigger impact on computing costs

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…
items.t: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris

items.title: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout
items.summary:
New draft text released at Cop31 summit after countries fail to agree on electrification and finance for developing world

Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels.

The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress.

Brady and Spiro, who is representing the planned Fifa investor Joshua Kushner in a legal battle against Uefa, would become limited partners in Clearlake with no voting rights at Chelsea if the transactions are completed.

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
items.t: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
